lesson.title: The Fourth Band: Living With Imperfect Resistors
lesson.summary: No two resistors off the same production line are exactly identical, and tolerance is the manufacturer's guarantee of how far a real part can stray from its printed value.
lesson.body:
Every resistor that comes off a production line is a little different from its neighbor. The carbon film, metal film, or wirewound element inside is manufactured to a target value, but tiny variations in material thickness, doping, and the length of the resistive track mean no two parts are perfectly identical. Tolerance is the manufacturer's promise about how far a real resistor is allowed to stray from its printed, nominal value, expressed as a plus or minus percentage. A resistor marked 1 kilohm with 5 percent tolerance is guaranteed to measure somewhere between 950 and 1050 ohms, even though the number printed or coded on its body says exactly 1000.

You already know how to read the value bands from the resistor color code. Tolerance rides along as one more band, usually the last one, set apart slightly from the value bands. Gold means 5 percent, silver means 10 percent, brown means 1 percent, red means 2 percent, and a resistor with no tolerance band at all defaults to 20 percent, the loose standard from decades ago that is rarely used in modern designs. The tighter the tolerance, the more precisely the factory has trimmed or selected that part, and the more it typically costs.

Consider a resistor with bands yellow, violet, red, gold. The first two bands give the significant digits 4 and 7, the third band multiplies by 100, so the nominal value is 47 times 100, or 4700 ohms. The gold band means 5 percent tolerance. Five percent of 4700 is 235, found by multiplying 4700 by 0.05. That means the actual resistance is guaranteed to fall between 4700 minus 235 and 4700 plus 235, or 4465 ohms to 4935 ohms. Any resistor pulled from that reel and measured with a multimeter should land inside that window, even though every one is stamped as a 4.7 kilohm part.

Tolerance is why component manufacturers do not sell every possible resistance value. Instead they sell a spaced set of nominal values called the E-series, such as E24 for 5 percent parts, where consecutive values are spread apart by roughly the tolerance percentage. This spacing means the guaranteed ranges of adjacent values just touch or slightly overlap, covering the entire span of possible resistances without wasting inventory on values so close together that tolerance would make them indistinguishable anyway.

Tolerance also compounds when resistors work together. In a voltage divider built from two 5 percent resistors, the output voltage can be off by more than 5 percent because both resistors can drift in opposite directions at once, and a careful designer checks the worst case combination rather than assuming errors cancel. For circuits where precision truly matters, such as reference voltage dividers in measurement instruments, engineers reach for 1 percent or even 0.1 percent metal film resistors, paying a premium in price for a guarantee that keeps the whole circuit behaving predictably.
